# Authentication

Construct a `dev.unofficialbox.Client` from one of the four Box auth flows, built
via `dev.unofficialbox.auth.Auth`. Each returns a
`dev.unofficialbox.runtime.Runtime.Auth` token source that caches its access token
until shortly before it expires; the network layer refreshes on a `401` and
retries once. (Config types below stay on `Runtime`, e.g. `Runtime.CcgConfig`.)

## Developer Token

```java
Client client = new Client(Auth.developerToken("DEVELOPER_TOKEN"));
```

## Client Credentials Grant (server auth, no key)

```java
Client client = new Client(Auth.clientCredentials(
        Runtime.CcgConfig.enterprise("CLIENT_ID", "CLIENT_SECRET", "ENTERPRISE_ID")));
// or Runtime.CcgConfig.user("CLIENT_ID", "CLIENT_SECRET", "USER_ID")
```

## JWT (server auth with a signing key)

```java
// From an app's box_config.json (bad key: fails loudly at construction):
Client client = new Client(Auth.jwt(Runtime.JwtConfig.fromBoxConfig(boxConfigJson)));
// or build it explicitly:
Runtime.JwtConfig config = Runtime.JwtConfig.enterprise(
        "CLIENT_ID", "CLIENT_SECRET", "PUBLIC_KEY_ID",
        privateKeyPem, keyPassphrase, "ENTERPRISE_ID");
Client client = new Client(Auth.jwt(config));
```

## OAuth 2.0 (authorization code)

Redirect the user to the consent URL and exchange the returned code. Box
rotates the refresh token on every refresh and rejects the old one, so pass a
`RefreshTokenStore` that writes it somewhere durable; it is called with the
token the exchange issues and with every rotation after. Later runs resume from
the newest saved token:

```java
Runtime.OAuthConfig oauth = new Runtime.OAuthConfig("CLIENT_ID", "CLIENT_SECRET");
// first run: redirect to oauth.authorizeUrl(redirectUri, state), then
// Auth auth = oauth.exchangeCode(code, redirectUri, tokenStore);
// later runs: resume from the newest saved refresh token.
Client client = new Client(Auth.oauthWithStore(oauth, newestSavedRefreshToken, tokenStore));
```

## Revoking a token

For logout or uninstall, `revokeToken()` revokes the token a CCG, JWT, or OAuth
flow holds — with the flow's own client credentials, at the revoke endpoint
beside its token URL, through its proxy — and clears it from the cache:

```java
Runtime.Auth auth = Auth.oauth(oauth, storedRefreshToken);
Client client = new Client(auth);
// … on logout:
auth.revokeToken();
```

A CCG or JWT flow acquires a fresh token on its next use. OAuth revokes the
whole grant: every later call throws, so discard the stored refresh token and
run the authorization-code flow again. A developer token has no client
credentials to revoke with (`revokeToken()` throws) — pass them yourself to
`client.authorization.revokeOauth2`.

## Acting as another user

An admin, or a service account whose app may *make API calls using the as-user
header*, can act as another user. `withAsUserHeader` returns a new client whose
every call sends Box's `As-User` header; it shares the original's auth (and
token cache) and configuration, and the original is unchanged:

```java
Client userClient = client.withAsUserHeader("USER_ID");
var me = userClient.users.getMe(null); // the user USER_ID
```

## Downscoping a token

Exchange the session's access token for one limited to `scopes` and,
optionally, to one item (its API URL) or shared link (pass `null` to skip
either) — e.g. to hand a browser-side preview a narrow token. The result has
no refresh token; build a client from it as a developer token:

```java
AccessToken down = client.authorization.downscopeToken(
        List.of("item_preview"), "https://api.box.com/2.0/files/123", null);
Client preview = new Client(Auth.developerToken(down.accessToken().orElseThrow()));
```
